The founders who are easiest to work with are not the ones with the best numbers. They are the ones who qualify their own sentences before anybody asks them to. I will give you the test I use, and it takes about four minutes. I ask a very open question: tell me about your clients. A founder who is not ready says we work with large enterprises across several sectors, and then he stops and waits for the next question. A founder who is ready says our two strongest sectors are these, our largest client came to us this way and has renewed this many times, and the part of the base I actually worry about is this one. Nobody made him say the last part. He said it because he has already had the argument with himself, and once you hear that, the rest of the meeting changes. You stop testing him and you start thinking with him, which is a completely different meeting and it is the one everybody says they want.

I want to say something about long sentences, because founders get told to keep everything short and it is bad advice in this specific room. Short is right when you are pitching to a crowd. In diligence you are not pitching, you are being examined, and a short sentence in an examination is a sentence somebody else gets to finish for you. Watch what happens. You say we have a strong backlog. That is short, and now the analyst decides what strong means, and she will decide conservatively, because that is her job. Say instead: we have a backlog of this size, of which this much is under signed contract and the rest is verbal, and it sits mostly in the vertical where our delivery record is longest. That is one sentence. It is not complicated English. But there is now nothing left in it for anybody else to fill in, and the number you said is the number that goes into the model.
